patient.name: Tomasz Nowak
patient.complaint: Low back pain shooting down the back of his left leg for 10 days
background: Warehouse worker; pain began lifting a heavy box
Previous episodes of mechanical back pain
No weight loss, fever or cancer history

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which nerve root is most likely affected?' or 'Which is the most likely finding on examination?' with a dermatome, a weak myotome and a lost reflex; or 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with red flags that make it cauda equina.

points: Tomasz, 41, felt a twinge lifting a box 10 days ago.
Now **pain shoots from buttock down the back of his left leg** to the foot.
Leg pain is worse than back pain; coughing makes it worse.
Numb outer edge of his left foot.

steps.lead: Tomasz's pain follows one root down the leg after lifting: a lumbar **disc prolapse** causing **sciatica**.
Each root has its own **dermatome**, **myotome** and **reflex**, so examination tells you the level.

points: **Straight leg raise** reproduces leg pain at 40° on the left.
Weak plantarflexion: cannot tiptoe-walk on the left.
**Left ankle reflex absent**; knee reflexes normal.
Numb posterior calf and lateral foot.

visual.label: Tomasz 40°
visual.caption: Leg pain between 30° and 70° on raising the straight leg: a positive sciatic stretch test (L5/S1 roots).

steps.q: Absent ankle reflex, weak plantarflexion, numb lateral foot. Which root?
steps.r: **S1**: ankle reflex, plantarflexion, posterior leg and lateral foot. L5 gives foot drop with normal reflexes.

steps.lead: Tomasz fits **S1** exactly. Learn each root by its pain, weak movement, numb skin and reflex.

No saddle numbness; passing urine and stool normally.

steps.lead: Tomasz has no red flags, but back pain with **urinary retention** or **saddle anaesthesia** is **cauda equina** until proven otherwise.

visual.title: Which reflex tests which root?
visual.label: Tomasz: ankle reflex lost
visual.caption: Ankle = S1, knee = L3/L4, triceps = C7, biceps and supinator = C5/C6.

glossary.radiculopathy: Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root causing pain, numbness or weakness in its territory.
glossary.nerve root: The part of a spinal nerve where it leaves the spinal canal.
glossary.sciatica: Pain radiating down the back of the leg from a lumbar or sacral nerve root, usually a disc prolapse.
glossary.dermatome: The area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve root.
glossary.myotome: The group of muscles supplied by one spinal nerve root.
glossary.disc prolapse: Herniation of the soft disc centre through its outer ring, which can press on a nerve root.
glossary.disc herniation: Another name for a disc prolapse.
glossary.nucleus pulposus: The soft gel centre of an intervertebral disc.
glossary.annulus fibrosus: The tough outer ring of an intervertebral disc.
glossary.posterolateral: Behind and to the side; the commonest direction of disc prolapse.
glossary.straight leg raise: Raising the straight leg stretches the L5/S1 roots; leg pain between 30° and 70° is positive.
glossary.sciatic nerve stretch test: Straight leg raise test for L5/S1 root irritation.
glossary.foot drop: Inability to dorsiflex the ankle, so the foot slaps or catches.
glossary.slapping gait: Foot slaps the floor on each step because of weak dorsiflexion.
glossary.patellar reflex: Knee jerk reflex, tested by tapping the patellar tendon (L3/L4).
glossary.brachioradialis reflex: Supinator reflex at the wrist, C5/C6.
glossary.supinator reflex: Another name for the brachioradialis reflex (C5/C6).
glossary.plantarflexion: Pointing the foot down, as in standing on tiptoes (S1).
glossary.dorsiflexion: Lifting the foot upwards at the ankle (L4/L5).
glossary.inversion: Turning the sole of the foot inwards (L4/L5, tibial nerve).
glossary.eversion: Turning the sole of the foot outwards (superficial peroneal nerve).
glossary.cauda equina: Bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord.
glossary.cauda equina syndrome: Compression of the cauda equina causing saddle anaesthesia, sphincter disturbance and bilateral leg signs.
glossary.saddle anaesthesia: Numbness of the perineum, buttocks and inner thighs.
glossary.urinary retention: Inability to empty the bladder; often painless in cauda equina.
glossary.anal tone: Resting tightness of the anal sphincter, checked on rectal examination.
glossary.conus medullaris: The tapering end of the spinal cord, around L1/L2.
glossary.LMN: Lower motor neurone; lesions cause weakness, reduced tone and reduced reflexes.
glossary.UMN: Upper motor neurone; lesions cause increased tone and brisk reflexes.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as naproxen or ibuprofen.
glossary.amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for neuropathic pain.
glossary.neuropathic pain: Burning, shooting or electric pain from damaged nerves.
glossary.epidural steroid injection: Steroid injected near the nerve root to reduce inflammation.
glossary.decompression: Surgery to remove the structure pressing on nerve roots.
glossary.common peroneal palsy: Injury to the nerve at the fibular head, giving foot drop with inversion spared.
glossary.ABPI: Ankle brachial pressure index; below 0.9 suggests peripheral arterial disease.
glossary.MRC: Medical Research Council 0 to 5 scale of muscle power.
